To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the functional characterization of novel MCAD variants can be performed in vitro and that the results can be used for individual patient management.

we have identified 15 novel MCAD mutations with severely decreased residual activities, and three novel mutations with only moderately decreased residual activities, all of which have been functionally characterized in vitro for the first time.
the functional characterization of novel mutations is essential for the individual management of patients after NBS and that our results provide the basis for such an approach.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of novel mutations, the identification of novel molecular chaperones for MCAD, and the elucidation of the three-dimensional structure of MCAD.
the functional characterization of 18 heterozygous MCAD variants and their classification as either severe or moderate.
the characterization of the molecular basis for MCAD deficiency and the classification of novel mutations in the context of their clinical relevance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the majority of mutations in ACADM cause severe MCAD deficiency.
a residual enzyme activity < 5 %, even with high expression levels, is a good indicator of MCAD deficiency.
a residual activity of <5 % is a strong indication of MCAD deficiency, whereas a residual activity of >20 % indicates a mild phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mutations in the ACADM coding region that cause MCAD deficiency are not only those with a complete loss of function.
all MCAD variants should be characterized functionally in vitro to obtain a more complete understanding of their pathogenicity.

mutations in the ACADM protein that affect the active site or the substrate binding region are likely to cause MCAD deficiency, whereas mutations that affect the protein structure in other areas may be classified as variants of unknown clinical relevance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
some mutations that are classified as pathogenic in the literature are actually benign and do not affect the protein function.
a combination of different assays, such as temperature-dependent and chaperone-dependent assays, is required to classify a mutant.
some variants that are not associated with a disease phenotype in NBS may be associated with a disease in the future.
